alex_k: Heads-up — customer INC-9876 (healthtech) says a bunch of their streaming requests were marked 5xx and billed. They claim their client closed the connection (FIN) shortly after receiving final tokens, but our metrics show gateway 5xx increments. Repro steps + logs below.
maria_s: Oof. Can you paste the gateway logs and the customer's request ID? We need to see whether the proxy returned a 502/504 or if our recorder flagged it as a server error.
alex_k: Request IDs: req=cl-7a9f2 / gw=gw-45c2b. Customer repro:
1) Open streaming request to /v1/streams
2) Receive final chunk
3) Client sends FIN immediately -> connection closed within ~30ms
4) Customer sees 5xx in billing portal and charged for tokens after FIN
Logs (gateway) — note the short gap and half-close:
```
[2026-03-10T14:23:12.105Z] gw-45c2b INFO accept conn from 10.12.3.45
[2026-03-10T14:23:12.212Z] gw-45c2b INFO proxy -> backend req cl-7a9f2 started
[2026-03-10T14:23:12.512Z] gw-45c2b INFO backend -> proxy streaming chunk "..."
[2026-03-10T14:23:12.540Z] gw-45c2b INFO connection half-closed by client (FIN)
[2026-03-10T14:23:12.541Z] gw-45c2b WARN upstream socket reset; treating as 502
[2026-03-10T14:23:12.542Z] gw-45c2b METRIC increment 5xx_streaming=1
```
jamie_v: That increment at 14:23:12.542 is the problem. We currently treat any upstream socket reset during streaming as a gateway 5xx to be safe, but in cases where the client closed after receiving last chunk we should probably treat that as a client-initiated close (no 5xx) and not bill. Is there a spec we can use to distinguish FIN vs unexpected RST?
ingrid: I dug into the proxy code — it conflates EINPROGRESS/EPIPE/read 0 semantics and emits a single path that increments the 5xx counter. There's no TTL on how long after the final chunk we accept a FIN as normal. Customer said they close <50ms after final token.
ops-bot: Incident created INC-9876-streaming-billing-escalation, priority=P2, linked ticket: TKT-5421
maria_s: Can we reproduce locally with curl or a small client that closes right after reading final chunk? If so, add test to proxy that a FIN within X ms of last write should be interpreted as client normal close.
alex_k: Repro script I used (node) — essentially read streaming chunks then socket.end() after 25ms. I'll paste below:
```
const net = require('net');
// pseudo-code: open TLS->gateway, read until we see 'data: [DONE]', setTimeout(() => socket.end(), 25)
```
jamie_v: I ran a quick local run and reproduced. The issue occurs when the backend has already flushed tokens and the client tears down during the final write/flush handshake. Proxy sees write EPIPE or early FIN and maps to upstream failure. Two paths forward:
1) Short-term: change billing pipeline to exclude 5xx increments when the connection closes within 200ms of the last successful write + backend reported 'complete'. That avoids charging customers while we push code.
2) Medium-term: update proxy to differentiate client-close-after-complete vs mid-stream upstream error. Need to add a small handshake marker between backend and gateway at stream completion (e.g., backend emits DONE_ACK) so gateway knows final state.
eng-runtime: @jamie_v can you open a PR with an instrumentation flag first? We want logs gated and a rollout to canary. If old behavior persists we might miscount in other edge cases. Also include unit tests for the <200ms heuristic.
jamie_v: Will do. I'll add a feature flag `proxy.treat_close_post_complete_as_client` and default it off. Also will add a metrics label `close_after_complete=true|false` so billing can filter historic increments.
maria_s: For the billing side I'll file a job to reclassify the affected increments for INC-9876 and refund the customer if they were charged. TKT-5422 created.
alex_k: Customer update note — we'll do the reclassification and follow up once the PR lands in canary. Thanks everyone. :thumbsup:

eng-runtime: Following — will review the PR and coordinate canary window. Also recommend we add a synthetic test in production that simulates a quick FIN after final chunk, to avoid regression.
